questions.question: The classical EOQ model assumes constant deterministic demand, instantaneous batch replenishment, no shortages, a fixed setup cost per order and a holding cost per unit per unit time. Which situation violates these assumptions?
options: Customers wait for the next batch when stock runs out.
Each order incurs a fixed charge regardless of its size.
Stock is charged per unit held per unit of time.
The whole batch arrives at once when it is ordered.

questions.question: In the classical EOQ cost rate $TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}$, with demand rate $D$, setup cost $K$, holding cost $h$ per unit per unit time and batch size $y$, what does $\frac{hy}{2}$ represent?
options: The holding cost of one cycle, from average stock $\frac{y}{2}$
The holding cost per unit time of the full batch $y$
The cost of buying half a batch at unit price $h$
The holding cost rate, from average stock $\frac{y}{2}$

questions.question: In the classical EOQ model all demand $D$ is met and every unit costs the same constant price $c$. Why can the purchasing cost rate $cD$ be left out of $TCU(y)$ when choosing the batch size $y$?
options: It is already included in the setup cost $K$ of each order.
It is equal for every $y$, so it cannot move the best $y$.
It is usually negligible next to setup and holding costs.
It is paid only once, for the very first batch.

questions.question: In the classical EOQ model with $TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}$, what happens to the two cost components as the batch size $y$ increases?
options: Both cost rates fall, since larger batches are cheaper per unit
Fewer setups per unit time, but more stock held on average
Both cost rates rise, since more is ordered at a time
Only the holding rate changes; setups stay as frequent

questions.question: For $K,D,h>0$, why does $TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}$ have its smallest value at some finite batch size $y>0$?
options: Both terms grow with $y$, so the cost is smallest close to $y=0$.
Both terms shrink with $y$, so the cost is smallest for very large $y$.
The setup term grows without bound near $y=0$, the holding term for large $y$.
The cost is linear in $y$, so it is smallest at an end of the range.

questions.question: A shop uses the classical EOQ model with setup cost $K=100$ euros per order, demand $D=50$ units per week and holding cost $h=2$ euros per unit per week. What is $TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}$ for batch size $y=100$?
options: 250 euros per week
50 euros per week
150 euros per week
5100 euros per week

questions.question: A classical EOQ setting has $K=50$ euros per order, $D=20$ units per day and $h=1$ euro per unit per day. Among the batch sizes 20, 40 and 80, which gives the lowest $TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}$?
options: $y=80$, with the lowest setup cost rate
$y=20$, with the lowest holding cost rate
$y=20$, with cost rate 12.5 per day
$y=40$, with cost rate 45 per day

questions.question: A classical EOQ setting has $K=26$ euros per order, demand $D=100$ units per week and holding cost $h=5.20$ euros per unit per year, with 52 weeks per year. What is $TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}$ in euros per week for $y=200$?
options: 533 euros per week
1196 euros per week
23 euros per week
33 euros per week

questions.question: A classical EOQ setting has $K=200$ euros per order, $D=10$ units per day and $h=1$ euro per unit per day, with current batch size $y=40$. Does doubling the batch size to $y=80$ lower $TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}$?
options: No, from 70 up to 90 euros per day
No, it stays at 70 euros per day
Yes, from 70 to 65 euros per day
Yes, from 70 to 45 euros per day

questions.question: A classical EOQ stock graph shows stock falling linearly from 30 units to 0 every 6 days, with instant refills. The setup cost is 60 euros per order and the holding cost 2 euros per unit per day. What is the relevant cost per day?
options: 70 euros per day
240 euros per day
25 euros per day
40 euros per day

questions.question: In the classical EOQ model with $TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}$, the holding cost $h$ rises while $K$ and $D$ stay the same. How does the batch size that makes $TCU$ smallest move?
options: It falls, as stock has become dearer to hold.
It rises, as each unit now costs more to hold.
It stays put, as $h$ does not affect setup costs.
It falls to zero, as holding outweighs setups.

questions.question: For a classical EOQ setting, $TCU(y)$ is smallest over all positive real $y$ at $y=48.3$, but batches must be whole boxes. Which batch sizes must be compared to find the best whole number?
options: Only 48, the whole number nearest to 48.3
Only 49, rounding up so that stock lasts longer
Any whole number, as $TCU$ is flat near its minimum
48 and 49, the whole numbers on either side of 48.3

questions.question: A shop's weekly demand averages 100 units but varies from week to week, and it applies the classical EOQ model with $D=100$ units per week. Which statement about this use of the mean is correct?
options: Using the mean gives the same policy as modelling the variation.
The mean already captures the variation, as it averages over it.
The model needs the largest weekly demand instead of the mean.
The model uses only the mean, so variation is not reflected.

questions.question: A classical EOQ setting has $K=100$ euros per order, $D=40$ units per day and $h=2$ euros per unit per day, with current batch size $y=50$. Using the derivative of $TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}$, should $y$ be increased or decreased to lower the cost?
options: Decrease $y$, since $TCU'(50)=0.6$
Increase $y$, since $TCU'(50)=-0.6$
Decrease $y$, since $TCU'(50)=2.6$
Keep $y$, since $TCU'(50)=1$

questions.question: A classical EOQ setting has $K=50$ euros per order, $D=10$ units per day and $h=1$ euro per unit per day. With batch size $y=40$, what are the setup and holding costs of one ordering cycle?
options: 130 euros per cycle
32.5 euros per cycle
70 euros per cycle
210 euros per cycle

questions.question: A classical EOQ setting has $K=50$ euros per order, $D=20$ units per day, $h=1$ euro per unit per day and batch size $y=50$. If demand doubles to 40 units per day while $y$ stays at 50, what is the new $TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}$?
options: 65 euros per day
90 euros per day
45 euros per day
70 euros per day

questions.question: In the classical EOQ model the holding cost is assumed to satisfy $h>0$. What would happen to the choice of batch size if $h=0$, with $K,D>0$?
options: Any $y$ is optimal, since holding is free.
No best $y$: the cost keeps falling as $y$ grows.
The best $y$ is the one where $\frac{KD}{y}=0$.
The best $y$ is as small as possible, to keep stock low.

questions.question: A shop follows a classical EOQ policy with batch size $y$, but each new batch arrives when 10 units are still in stock, so stock moves between 10 and $y+10$. Which part of $TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}$ is now wrong, and how?
options: $\frac{KD}{y}$ is too low: orders now come more often.
$\frac{hy}{2}$ is too low: stock averages $\frac{y}{2}+10$.
$\frac{hy}{2}$ is too high: the batch is partly old stock.
Neither: the 10 spare units are used in the next cycle.

questions.question: A classical EOQ setting has $K=50$ euros per order, $D=40$ units per day and $h=2.2$ euros per unit per day, giving $TCU(40)=94$ and $TCU(50)=95$ euros per day. Since $TCU$ is strictly convex on $y>0$, what do these two values alone show about its minimum point?
options: It lies below 50.
It lies below 40.
It is exactly 40.
It lies above 50.

questions.question: A classical EOQ setting has $K=25$ euros per order, $D=81$ units per day and $h=2$ euros per unit per day, so $TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}$ is smallest over positive reals at $y=45$. Batches must be whole pallets of 10 units. Which batch size is best?
options: 40, rounding down from the halfway point 45
Either 40 or 50, as 45 lies exactly between them
50, since $TCU(50)$ comes out below $TCU(40)$
45, the point where $TCU$ is smallest over the reals
